newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - High NZD tensions unlikely to disappear.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - High NZD tensions unlikely to disappear.

text.p: By Paul Stewart, Chief Economist at ANZ Bank (NZ)
WELLINGTON, Dec 16 - The strength of the New Zealand dollar is starting to bite.
The best barometer of that is not to be found in official statistics but in the increasingly vocal and public discussion about its impact upon the export sector.

Even during his coalition announcement, Winston Peters reiterated that reducing pressure on the NZ dollar is a priority, although there was nothing in the initial cut of policy that addresses the issue directly.
Even so, Mr Peters may be encouraged by market developments in the near term. There can be no doubt that interest rates have had a major bearing on the NZ dollar's value in recent times.
The level of euro-kiwi and dual currency issuance throughout 1996 is evidence enough that global investors find our short term yields attractive.

However, with the RBNZ now operating to the wider 0-3 percent inflation target with a higher mid-point of 1.5 percent, the central bank is likely to tolerate slightly easier monetary conditions in the near term.
Any significant reduction in the differential between New Zealand and world short term interest rates will take the gloss off the kiwi.
However, with financial markets generally encouraged by political developments, a sharp correction in the New Zealand dollar is unlikely.
Consequently, any hiatus in political and public pressure to relieve the economy of exchange rate stresses may prove to be short-lived.
Michael Cullen is another who is not only concerned about, but purports to have some highly orthodox and commonly practised ways of addressing the overvalued exchange rate.
Now destined to remain in opposition, Labour may not get the opportunity to implement Dr Cullen's ideas, but that does not mean they will not receive a further public airing.
When pressed, Dr Cullen has said calls for dropping interest rates missed the point, but to date, he has refused to go into detail.

What might these solutions to the overvalued exchange rate be? One suggestion has been that a non-resident withholding tax on bonds could be reintroduced. Indeed, that may well be effective in dampening the NZ dollar because a NRWT would certainly reduce the attractiveness of New Zealand bonds to offshore investors.
However, the flip-side is the long term impact of higher borrowing costs for the government and potentially, other New Zealand entities. The new government has already moved to discount this option.

Another option, which has certainly been inferred from Dr Cullen's comments, is direct intervention in foreign exchange markets. This tool, one which is already available to the RBNZ, has been used by other central banks and proved quite popular in the 1980s.
The process itself, known as "sterilised intervention", is quite straightforward.

Under current circumstances, where the objective would be to lower the exchange rate, the RBNZ would sell NZ dollars into the market and buy foreign currency (probably US dollars) which would then be invested in foreign currency securities (say US
Treasury bonds).

The RBNZ would then soak up the excess liquidity created by the additional NZ dollars by issuing local securities such as treasury bills (not to do so would increase the money supply, which would be inflationary).
In effect, the exchange rate should be pushed down and interest rates up.

Some might think it odd that the RBNZ has not already employed this tactic. After all, they have repeatedly stated that their preferred mix of monetary conditions at present (given current sources of inflation), is for higher interest
rates and a lower exchange rate.
Why then has the RBNZ chosen not to directly intervene when financial markets have been pushing the mix in the opposite direction?
We do not know for sure, but it is a fair bet that the RBNZ Governor and other officials do not believe it would work.
Indeed, there is a large body of empirical research which suggests that to the extent sterilised intervention has any impact, its effect is not significant nor lasting.

Intuition suggests that central bank intervention should influence a currency's value. After all, central banks are large players and are likely to be dealing in substantial sums of money. And indeed, typically they are.
For example, between July and September 1992, when Europe's ERM was under strain, central bank intervention is estimated to have totalled over US$160 billion (three times New Zealand's GDP).
Critically though, even this pales into insignificance compared to total market activity. According to a BIS survey, daily turnover in foreign exchange markets in 1995 was around US$1.6 trillion.

Although for New Zealand the volumes are much less (daily turnover of NZ dollars was estimated at US$3-4 billion), the principle is the same. In absolute terms, central bank activity will be swamped by total market flows.
Consequently, central bank intervention can only work to the extent that it changes market sentiment and expectations.
Rather than recite the research results verbatim, it is perhaps simpler to use them to look at the likely course of events if the RBNZ were to break its habit and intervene.

The initial intervention would almost certainly have some impact upon the NZ dollar. Markets would be taken by surprise (an announcement effect) and would be unclear whether the Reserve Bank was signalling something new about monetary policy. If the market associated intervention with a change in monetary policy, the size and duration of an announcement effect would be greater.

However, assuming the RBNZ's view on inflation had not altered (that is, the intervention was intended only to influence the interest rate/exchange rate mix) and they reasserted that view, the effect would soon dissipate since the fundamental factors underpinning the value of the NZ dollar would remain intact.
Based on international experience, the full duration of the impact may be no longer than a few days. Futhermore, subsequent interventions are likely to have even less effect upon the exchange rate.
Of course, the announcement of intervention is likely to have a greater impact if market fundamentals were moving, or were beginning to move in a manner consistent with the thrust of intervention.
Consequently, it could have greater impact now, when the markets are starting to anticipate some softening in monetary policy by the RBNZ.

However, if the RBNZ did want to signal a change in policy settings, under the current framework it could achieve a very similar result by simply making a statement to that effect: in Tuesday's Monetary Policy Statement, for example.

Finally, intervention carries with it some costs and risks. Whilst sterilised intervention appears not to have any lasting effect, some research suggests that it may increase day to day volatility in foreign exchange markets.
That would seem to run counter to the over-riding objective of promoting stable economic growth and price stability.
And of course there have been some celebrated cases where central banks have incurred heavy financial losses through their intervention practises.
Notably, it is estimated that its defence of the British pound during the ERM debacle may have cost the Bank of England in excess of GBP 5 billion as sterling fell in value.
To my mind there are no quick fix solutions to the NZ dollar strength if we remain serious about maintaining low inflation.

However, just as foreign exchange dealers are sometimes reminded when their egos are running ahead of them, we might well recall a quotation by Winston Churchill: "There is no sphere of human thought in which it is easier for a man to show superficial cleverness and the appearance of superior wisdom than in discussing questions of currency and exchange."
